transcript.content: Hello. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, hi. Um... so, I guess I came in because things have been getting really... tangled up lately, especially with my work. I do a lot of commission work and gallery shows, so communication is a huge part of what I do. But recently, when I sit down to write my artist statements for a new exhibition, or even just when I'm trying to type up basic client notes after a consultation, it's like my brain just won't stay on a straight track. 

I'll start off writing about something practical, like the textures I'm using, you know, the physical feel of the canvas or the layering of the paint, but then mid-sentence I'm suddenly going on about the materials budget, and then before I even realize it, I'm deep into explaining these intense, secret meanings behind the brushstrokes that are hidden in the piece. And it's not just when I'm writing, either. Even what I say out loud in meetings with clients or curators has started jumping around exactly like that—from textures to budgets to secret meanings—and it's getting really embarrassing. 

People just kind of stare at me, and they keep telling me they can’t follow what I’m trying to explain. It makes perfect sense to me while I'm saying it, the connections are all right there in my head, but apparently, to everyone else, it's just this confusing maze and they can't understand me at all. It's just incredibly frustrating to feel like you're explaining your vision perfectly and everyone else is just lost.
About how long have you been noticing these changes in your thinking and speech?

Well, let me think about the exact timeline, because it's actually really tied to my career trajectory, I think. It’s been right about... a year and two months, I’d say. Yes, exactly a year and two months, because that was right around the time I made this massive shift in my professional life. 

I used to do community curation, which was honestly wonderful, you know, organizing local artists, setting up neighborhood galleries, dealing with city grants and all that heavy administrative stuff that keeps you really grounded. But I really, really wanted to focus on my own physical pieces, so I took the leap and switched into full-time independent installation work. And it was right around that exact transition, about fourteen months ago, that I started noticing the threads getting crossed. 

I remember my first big independent project right after I left the curation job, I was trying to map out the spatial dimensions for this suspended wire piece, and my notes just started unraveling into these long tangents about the metallic sourcing and what the wire actually meant for society, instead of just writing down the measurements. So yeah, about a year and two months, ever since I left the community curation job to do my own installations full-time. It’s just been this constant, frustrating build-up since then, which is so ironic because you'd think working for yourself without a boss would make your thoughts clearer and give you more space, not make everything more tangled up, but it really just started right when I made that switch.

Doctor, that's... well, that's a really interesting question, actually, because there's this whole other side to what's been happening, and it's not just the tangled thoughts. It's like my energy and my mood go through these incredible, intense shifts. 

There will be these stretches of time, maybe a week or two, where I just feel completely lit up from the inside. It's this electric feeling, like I'm almost unstoppable. I'll be in my studio, and every single idea that pops into my head feels absolutely brilliant, like I'm finally tapping into some universal truth with my installations. I'll be working on three different pieces at once, convinced they're masterpieces, and I feel so good, so energized and elevated. 

But the flip side of that—and this is what really gets me into trouble—is that during those exact same periods, I get so unbelievably irritable. It's like my skin is too tight. If I'm working with a collaborator, or even just talking to a supplier about materials, and they make one tiny comment, just a small suggestion or a slight criticism, I will just snap. And I mean really snap. I get so angry, so fast, and the reaction is just completely out of proportion to whatever they actually said. It feels so much bigger than the situation warrants. 

Like last month, a lighting tech suggested moving a spotlight two inches to the left on a piece I was finishing, and I absolutely tore into him, just went on and on about how he was destroying my vision. It was awful, and I felt terrible later, but in the moment, when I'm in that lit-up, high-energy state, the irritation is just right there, sitting on the surface, ready to explode over the smallest little thing. So yes, it's this combination of feeling incredibly brilliant and elevated, but also being just a hair-trigger away from snapping at anyone who gets in my way.
Does this tangled thinking and jumping between topics happen even during times when your mood and energy feel completely normal?

Well, yes, actually. That's the part that really confuses me the most, I think. Because you'd assume—or at least I assumed—that the weird thoughts and the tangled words would only happen when my brain is running at a million miles an hour and I'm feeling all electric and irritable, right? But that's not how it works at all. 

Like, there was this one stretch recently, maybe just a month or so ago, where things actually got really quiet for me. I was sleeping a normal amount, maybe seven or eight hours a night, which is huge for me, and I wasn't waking up feeling like I needed to conquer the art world before breakfast. I didn't have that unstoppable, brilliant feeling at all. I was just... normal. Just going to the studio, drinking my tea, doing the work. 

But even then, even during that really quiet, stable month, the strange stuff was still happening. And it wasn't just the tangled writing, either. I would be sitting there, completely calm, mixing paints or whatever, and I would clearly hear these comments coming from right behind the storage shelves. Like, actual voices critiquing what I was doing, even though I was completely alone in the building. And I'd be looking at my ordinary studio materials, just regular canvas or masking tape, and I would start reading these incredibly intense, hidden warnings into them. Like the way the tape was peeling meant I was in danger, or the weave of the canvas was trying to tell me something terrible was about to happen. 

And that went on for several weeks, right in the middle of me feeling totally fine mood-wise. So, yeah, it's not just when I'm elevated or angry. It's like those thoughts and those... experiences... they just kind of live there on their own, even when the rest of me is completely quiet and just trying to have a normal day at work. It makes it so hard to trust my own environment, you know? Because I'll think, "Okay, I'm calm today, I'm good," and then suddenly the masking tape is sending me a message.
